text:
Pittsburgh Regional Transit Plans to Permanently Close Wabash Tunnel

PITTSBURGH
–
Pittsburgh Regional Transit plans to permanently close the Wabash Tunnel on December 1, pending approval by the PRT Board next week.

Keeping the tunnel open for long-term use would require an estimated $43 million in rehabilitation, in 2025 dollars. Following a comprehensive evaluation of the tunnel’s condition, safety, and long-term viability, PRT is recommending that the tunnel be decommissioned and closed to traffic.

PRT’s Board will consider the proposal at its regularly scheduled meeting on Friday, October 23.

“The Wabash Tunnel has a long history in Pittsburgh, but today it primarily serves private vehicle traffic rather than public transit,” said PRT CEO Katharine Kelleman. “With an estimated $43 million needed to rehabilitate the tunnel, we have a responsibility to focus our limited resources on the infrastructure that is most critical to delivering safe, reliable transit service.”

The tunnel was originally constructed in 1903 as part of the Wabash-Pittsburg Terminal Railroad. PRT, then the Port Authority of Allegheny County, acquired the tunnel in 1996 and converted it into a paved roadway facility with the use of federal transit funding. It reopened in 2004 as a High Occupancy Vehicle facility and was later opened to all traffic in 2017.

Today, the tunnel primarily serves private vehicle traffic and about 1,500 vehicles use the tunnel each day. PRT no longer provides scheduled transit service through the tunnel and has used it only as a detour route when regular bus service has been disrupted by roadwork or special events.

While the overall tunnel structure remains in fair condition, several critical components, including lighting, ventilation, and electrical systems, are in poor to critical condition and have exceeded their useful life. Keeping the tunnel open would require significant rehabilitation to meet current safety standards.

The closure will not affect the Wabash Park and Ride, which will remain open and continue to serve customers.

PRT requested and received concurrence from the Federal Transit Administration earlier this year to close the tunnel and retain the $848,238 in remaining federal funding value associated with the tunnel. That amount reflects the portion of the tunnel’s original federally funded value that remains after depreciation. The funds will be applied toward a future eligible federally funded PRT capital project.

###

text:
City Celebrates Opening of New McKinley Park Community Grove

Published on October 24, 2026

City of Pittsburgh and Pittsburgh Parks Conservancy Celebrate Opening of New McKinley Park Community Grove

New gathering space transforms historic Chicken Hill site into a welcoming destination for recreation, learning, and community connection

Pittsburgh, PA –
The City of Pittsburgh and Pittsburgh Parks Conservancy today celebrated the opening of the new McKinley Park Community Grove, marking the completion of a nearly $700,000 investment in a historic neighborhood gathering space in one of Pittsburgh’s oldest parks.

Neighbors, community partners, and park supporters gathered for a ribbon-cutting celebration at the Community Grove, located in the Chicken Hill section of McKinley Park just below Michigan Street.

Once home to a beloved, resident-built baseball field, the site has been transformed into a flexible, nature-based gathering space designed for recreation, education, and community connection while honoring the history and character of the neighborhood.

"Our community parks are important places that bring families and neighbors together to enjoy, play and connect," said Mayor O'Connor. "The new Community Grove at McKinley Park is a great community-driven project that honors the history of the park while creating new opportunities for future generations. Thanks to the community and the Pittsburgh Parks Conservancy for their partnership on this investment at McKinley."

Serving the Hilltop neighborhoods of Beltzhoover, Allentown, Knoxville, Bon Air, and surrounding communities, McKinley Park has long been an essential neighborhood green space. The Community Grove represents another significant step in the park’s ongoing revitalization following the adoption of the McKinley Park Master Plan in 2016.

“I’m so thankful to see this investment come to life, especially because it was driven every step of the way by the people who actually live here,” said Bob Charland, District 3, Pittsburgh City Councilman. “McKinley Park is one of Pittsburgh’s oldest parks, and its history means a lot to this neighborhood. For years, when Beltzhoover and Knoxville residents weren't welcomed or comfortable at other parks, Chicken Hill was their place. It was a site built by neighbors, for neighbors. The new Community Grove honors that history and brings back a natural gathering spot where our community can come together once again.”

Developed in close collaboration with residents and community partners—including the Beltzhoover Consensus Group, Knoxville Community Council, Voices Against Violence, and Hilltop Alliance—the project reflects years of community input and a shared vision for the future of the park.

“The Community Grove has always been about creating a space that reflects the people who know and love McKinley Park,” said Catherine Qureshi, President and CEO of the Pittsburgh Parks Conservancy. “From the beginning, neighbors helped shape the vision for what this place could become. Today, we get to celebrate that vision becoming a reality and open a space where neighbors can gather, learn, play, and make new memories together.”

The completed Community Grove includes:

A 20-foot hexagonal shade pavilion and surrounding seat wall for community gatherings

Open lawn space for recreation and neighborhood use

A dedicated outdoor learning area for education and small-group programming

Improved trail connections, stairs, and pathways

Stormwater and drainage improvements to reduce erosion and improve the long-term usability of the site

Expanded ecological restoration areas

Preserved historic baseball backstop posts honoring the site’s past and offering an opportunity for future community-led art

While the Community Grove is officially open, its landscape will continue to evolve. Spring 2027 will bring seasonal growth and blooms, adding color and wildlife habitat as the landscape matures.

Funding for the project was provided in part through the City of Pittsburgh Parks Tax Trust Fund, with additional support from the Henry L. Hillman Foundation, Pennsylvania American Water, and the American Water Charitable Foundation.

"Neighborhood parks like McKinley are an indispensable part of what makes Pittsburgh a great city,” said David Roger, president of Henry L. Hillman Foundation. “We know that parks give neighborhoods their character and charm and McKinley offers something for everyone in the Hilltop. We especially liked that the new Community Grove was developed in response to neighborhood input. It's going to be a terrific and much-used new feature."

The Community Grove builds upon broader investments in McKinley Park, including improvements to approximately 1.5 miles of trails throughout the park, helping create stronger connections between park destinations and surrounding neighborhoods.

To learn more about the project, visit
https://pittsburghparks.org/mckinley-park-community-grove/
or
https://engage.pittsburghpa.gov/mckinley-park-community-grove
.

###

text:
City Announces Trick-or-Treat Hours and City Halloween Events

Published on October 08, 2026

City of Pittsburgh Announces Trick-or-Treat Hours and City Halloween Events

City to host Trick-or-Treat, Track & Treat, City Hall Haunted Crawl and First-Ever Halloween House Decorating Contest

Pittsburgh, PA –
With the spooky season upon the City of Pittsburgh, today Mayor Corey O’Connor announced Halloween events happening throughout the city, including the
City of Pittsburgh’s official trick-or-treat on October 31, 2026 from 5:30 – 7:30 PM.

“Pittsburghers love to celebrate Halloween and all of the fun annual community traditions for our kids, families and neighbors,” said Mayor O’Connor. “I want to thank the community organizations who host events and our whole City and CitiParks team for being creative and coming up with fun new ways to bring our neighborhoods together. Let’s all do our part to make sure our kids have a safe and fun Halloween.”

The City recommends the following safety tips for trick-or-treaters:

Include reflective tape, stickers or clip-on lights on costumes and bags for visibility

Make sure children can properly see through masks or make-up for safe street crossing

Check costumes to make sure there aren’t obstructions that could cause trips or falls

Keep an eye on the weather forecast and dress appropriately for a more comfortable evening

Walk on sidewalks rather than in the streets, watch for vehicles and parents should assist children when crossing streets

Carry lights or flashlights for additional visibility

Anyone driving during the trick-or-treat hours must use additional caution, care and vigilance. Slow down and increase your awareness of trick-or-treaters.

CitiParks Annual Track & Treat Event

The City’s Department of Parks & Recreation (CitiParks) will host their annual Track & Treat event on Saturday, October 24, 2026 from 12:00 – 4:00 PM at the Bud Harris Cycling Track at 1401 Washington Boulevard in Highland Park.

The free annual family healthy lifestyle event brings together families from all over Pittsburgh to enjoy bike decorating, bike safety instructions, games, refreshments, food trucks and more. Attendees can bring their own bike or borrow one.

A costume contest is held at 2:00 PM with winners across four age groups for funniest, scariest and most original costume.

Additional information about
Track & Treat can be found on the CitiParks website
.

Third Annual City Hall Haunted Crawl

The City will be opening the doors of the City-County Building at 414 Grant Street for the Third Annual City Hall Haunted Crawl on Wednesday, October 28, 2026 from 5:30 – 7:30 PM. The event is free and open to the public to join for Halloween fun!

Costumes are encouraged as kids, families, goblins and ghouls can make their way through the Grand Lobby of the City-County Building, where City departments will be hosting Halloween-themed stations, welcoming attendees and handing out treats. From the people who keep our neighborhoods safe to those who maintain our parks, streets and public spaces, the Haunted Crawl is a fun opportunity to meet the people who serve our city every day.

CitiParks Citywide Halloween House Decorating Contest

CitiParks is excited to announce Pittsburgh’s first citywide Halloween house decorating contest. Pittsburghers are invited to deck their homes with their most creative and spookiest decorations to claim the top awards.

Participants can decorate their individual home or property, or partner with their neighbors and/or whole blocks, in one of the following categories:

Spookiest Individual Home

Spookiest Street

Best Overall Decor

Most Creative Design

Public Vote

The Mayor’s Choice

Properties must be within the City of Pittsburgh and all who participate do so at their own expense.

Photos of decorated houses can be submitted on the
Pittsburgh Halloween House Decorating Contest Engage PGH page
between now and October 23, 2026. A committee in CitiParks will evaluate the fab-boo-lous submissions.

Public online voting will begin on October 24, 2026 following Track & Treat. Votes can be cast on the
Pittsburgh Halloween House Decorating Content Engage PGH webpage
until October 28. Winners will be announced on October 30, 2026.

“CitiParks is committed to beloved fall events like Track & Treat and expanding our programming across our parks, recreation centers, and senior centers,” said Director of Parks and Recreation Eric Sloan. “This new free event is a great will to build neighborhood pride across the city.”

More information is available on the
Pittsburgh Halloween House Decorating Competition’s Engage PGH webpage
.

CitiParks’ continues its fall and winter season with the Riverview Park 5K Run & Fitness Walk, Track & Treat, Gingerbread House Display and Competition, new seasonal hours at the Henry W. Oliver Bath House, and much more.
Visit the CitiParks website for more information on upcoming youth and family events
.

text:
PRT Board Approves Four-Year Labor Agreement with ATU Local 85

PITTSBURGH
–
Pittsburgh Regional Transit’s Board today approved a four-year collective bargaining agreement with Amalgamated Transit Union (ATU) Local 85, representing approximately 2,100 operators, mechanics, and other employees. The agreement includes wage increases totaling 15% over four years, changes to health insurance plans, and work rule improvements designed to increase efficiency and support the agency’s workforce.

The union ratified the agreement on Sunday, following negotiations that began in March. The previous four-year agreement expired on June 30, and the parties reached a tentative agreement on October 9.

“PRT’s mission to serve Allegheny County is driven by the employees who operate our vehicles, maintain our fleet, and keep our system running every day,” said PRT CEO Katharine Kelleman. “This agreement recognizes their contributions, supports our employees, and helps ensure we can attract and retain the qualified workforce we need to provide reliable service to our riders for years to come.”

The contract provides wage increases totaling 15% over four years, with raises of 4% in each of the first two years and 3.5% in each of the final two years. Under the new agreement, the starting wage for a new operator in 2027 will be nearly $34 an hour, with the top rate exceeding $40 an hour.

The agreement also shortens the pay progression for new hires. Effective January 1, 2027, employees subject to the new-hire progression will reach the top pay rate after 36 months, 12 months sooner than under the previous agreement. The change is intended to strengthen PRT’s ability to recruit and retain employees.

The agreement includes changes to health insurance plan design. The changes increase employee deductibles and copays for the first time since 2012 while helping PRT manage rising health care expenses.

Seasonal service adjustments will increase from three to four times a year, giving PRT greater flexibility to respond to changing ridership trends and better align service with rider needs.

The agreement includes several work-rule changes intended to improve service reliability and operational efficiency. These include establishing a standard one-hour call-off requirement for employees who are unable to report to work, replacing the previous rule, which varied based on how long it would take an employee to travel to work, and the establishment of a joint management-union committee, which will identify and evaluate additional opportunities to improve how maintenance work is assigned and completed throughout the transit system.

###

text:
Paving on Forbes Avenue in Uptown to Restrict Multiple Side Streets

PITTSBURGH
– Motorists traveling on Forbes Avenue in Uptown should expect traffic delays and temporary restrictions to multiple cross streets this week as Pittsburgh Regional Transit continues paving for the University Line project.

On Tuesday, October 20, PRT’s contractor will begin final milling and paving on both sides of Forbes Avenue between Jumonville Street and the Birmingham Bridge. Crews will work from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. daily, with the work expected to be completed by Saturday, October 24.

Crews will also mill and pave intersections along Forbes Avenue at Jumonville, Seneca, and Moultrie streets. Later in the week, paving will take place at the intersections of Forbes Avenue and Marion, Van Braam, Miltenberger, Gist, and Seneca streets. During this work:

- One travel lane will be remain open on Forbes Avenue.

- Access to affected cross streets will be temporarily restricted while crews are working.

- Brief restrictions are expected at Brady Street and the Birmingham Bridge on-ramp as paving equipment moves through the area.

- Bus boarding will be at street level only.  PRT will have flaggers and staff to assist riders boarding and exiting buses.

- Sidewalk and ADA access will be maintained  opposite each active work zone.

All work is weather dependent and subject to change.

Additional paving at other locations on Fifth and Forbes avenues in Uptown and Oakland will continue through the end of November.

These improvements are part of Phase II of the University Line project, which will strengthen connections between Downtown, Uptown, and Oakland while improving the overall travel experience for riders, pedestrians, and cyclists.

To learn more about each of the current construction locations, please visit the University Line Newshub at

prt-brt-newshub.prezly.com/
.

text:
Paving for The University Line Will Continue ﻿in Uptown and Oakland Next Week

PITTSBURGH
–
Pittsburgh Regional Transit (PRT) will continue roadway restoration work for the University Line bus rapid transit project next week, with milling and paving operations on Fifth Avenue between Craft Avenue and Kirkpatrick Street near the Birmingham Bridge beginning Monday, October 26.

Motorists should expect changing traffic patterns throughout the week as crews complete the work. Kirkpatrick Street will be closed at Fifth Avenue on Monday and Tuesday, with intermittent closures possible for the remainder of the week between 7 a.m. and 5 p.m.

Additionally the westbound Boulevard of the Allies on-ramp from Fifth Avenue will close for up to two hours on Friday, October 30, between 9 a.m. and 3 p.m. to accommodate milling and paving. Traffic on Fifth Avenue will shift between the left and right lanes as work progresses. One travel lane will remain open throughout construction.

Motorists are encouraged to allow for extra travel time and use caution in the zone.

Bus stops will remain in service during construction, but will be unable to pull up to the sidewalk so riders will need to board and exit at street level. PRT staff and flaggers will be on-site to assist.

All work is weather-dependent and subject to change. Paving on Fifth Avenue in Oakland is expected to continue through the end of November.

These improvements are part of Phase II of the University Line project, which will strengthen connections between Downtown, Uptown, and Oakland while improving the overall travel experience for riders, pedestrians, and cyclists.

For more details and weekly construction updates, visit the
https://prt-brt-newshub.prezly.com/category/the-university-line-news

Events & Activations
Contribute to the vibrancy of Downtown Pittsburgh by creating memorable experiences through large-scale festivals and everyday activations.

Picklesburgh

Picklesburgh is the annual celebration that goes beyond the dill pickle to bring unique eats, food demonstrations, children’s activities, live music, and more to the heart of Downtown Pittsburgh. The best part? There really is a giant flying pickle.
LEARN MORE

Oktoberfest

A vibrant blend of Bavarian tradition and Steel City spirit, this multi-day community event aims to honor the rich cultural traditions of Oktoberfest while showcasing the best of Pittsburgh’s local talent and businesses.
LEARN MORE

Peoples Gas Holiday Market

Experience a one-of-a-kind seasonal shopping village with wooden chalets brimming with high-quality gifts that you won’t find anywhere else.
LEARN MORE

Highmark Light Up Night

Kick off the holiday season with high-quality entertainment, free concerts, tree-lighting ceremonies, food trucks, magic, and more all through the Golden Triangle.
LEARN MORE

More PDP Events

View Calendar

Clean & Safe
Deliver well-maintained public spaces, provide hospitality to visitors, and offer outreach services to the unhoused, creating a welcoming, clean and safe environment for all.

On-Street Services

Our Clean, Outreach and Hospitality teams provide a very visible, uniformed, and welcoming on-street presence throughout our district.
LEARN MORE

Clean + Safe Forums

Quarterly community meetings that provide updates on our efforts to ensure Downtown remains a great place to live, work, and play.

Volunteer

Whether you’re a team of an individual who’s interested in making Downtown shine, we can craft a volunteer experience suited to your needs.
LEARN MORE

Constituent Services
Strengthen connections, support local business, and coalesce stakeholders to advocate for and build a stronger Downtown.

Become A MEMBER

We invite you to join our community of like-minded organizations, businesses, and individuals who are dedicated to making Downtown a place we can all take pride in.
LEARN MORE

Current Members

View your membership benefits, view our member directory, access the member portal, and more.
VIEW MEMBERSHIP DETAILS

Downtown Edge Card

Support local businesses and receive special offers, discounts, deals, and more.
LEARN MORE

Economic Growth
Accelerate Downtown Pittsburgh’s economic growth by leading data-driven advocacy and collaborative stakeholder engagement to promote a vibrant, economically diverse, and resilient neighborhood.

Downtown ACtivity Dashboard

To measure activity in Downtown, the PDP tracks metrics that help keep local stakeholders, leaders, and citizens informed on a monthly, quarterly, and annual basis.
LEARN MORE

Project Pop-Up

Project Pop-Up seeks to transform vacant storefronts into vibrant, activated spaces, creating new and exciting destinations in Downtown Pittsburgh.
LEARN MORE

Downtown Rent Abatement Program

This program aims to foster the development of new, independent businesses in Downtown by building on existing retail destination clusters or filling needed gaps in retail offerings.
LEARN MORE

State of Downtown Pittsburgh

A quarterly webinar series for landowners, developers, investors, community leaders, and the general public that offers analysis and insights on key topical areas impacting Downtown.
LEARN MORE

Downtown Placemaking Grant

The Pittsburgh Downtown Partnership’s (PDP) Placemaking Grant, with generous support from Citizens, encourages Pittsburghers to utilize and program our public spaces through community-focused events and activations.
LEARN MORE

Mobility & Transportation

As a Transportation Management Association (TMA), the PDP endeavors to improve access to and around Downtown for motorists, transit riders, bicyclists and pedestrians with a focus on safety issues and encouragement of multi-modal transportation.

Downtown Mobility Plan

The Mobility Plan seeks to pilot mobility improvement projects aimed at preparing Downtown for the significant revitalization that’s occurring as a result of more than $5.2 billion in real estate and transportation investment over the last decade.
LEARN MORE

Pedestrian Wayfinding

The Pittsburgh Pedestrian Wayfinding Project is a world-class wayfinding system that will enhance navigation, improve accessibility, and increase connectivity between the Pittsburgh neighborhoods of Downtown, Oakland, and North Side.
LEARN MORE

Construction & Road Closure Updates

Road closures can be painful, but we’re helping to ease the struggles of ongoing construction. We’re providing navigation tips to help you get to and from Downtown effortlessly.
VIEW UPDATES

Public Realm
Create beautiful, inviting streets and public spaces that foster community and support the needs of a diverse neighborhood.

Public Art

Working with artists year-round to bring vibrant, public art installations to life throughout Downtown.
LEARN MORE

Paris to Pittsburgh

A matching grant program to assist property and business owners with exterior enhancements to enhance the public realm.
LEARN MORE

Market Square

The PDP is overseeing the historic modernization of Market Square, incorporating it as a key component of the 2025-2028 Strategic Vision for Downtown.
LEARN MORE

Downtown Development Activity Meetings

A forum available for residents, business owners, property owners, and other stakeholders to learn more about proposed Downtown development projects and provide feedback before the project can move forward in the City’s planning and approval process.
LEARN MORE

Reports & Publications

Annual Report

Read our latest Annual Reports to learn more about our work and impact on Downtown Pittsburgh.
READ OUR ANNUAL REPORTS

Who We Are

Our Team

Jeremy Waldrup

President & CEO

Contact

pdp@downtownpittsburgh.com

Lynda Fairbrother: (412) 325-0162

Bio

In addition to leading the work of the PDP, Jeremy participated in the inaugural class of Lead Now, is a graduate of Leadership Pittsburgh Class XXXI and a board member of Pittsburgh Bike Share and the Pittsburgh Public Theater. He has also been recognized for numerous awards and recognitions including Bike Pittsburgh’s Advocate of the Year, Pittsburgh Business Times Fast Tracker, and member of Smart Business’s Smart 50.
Prior to joining the PDP, Jeremy worked to support economic development initiatives with the City of New York serving as Assistant Commissioner of District Development for the Department of Small Business Services. In this role Jeremy was responsible for the oversight and capacity building of the City’s 64 Business Improvement Districts and investing in commercial revitalization projects through an annual grant-making program to local economic development organizations.
Jeremy also worked in business support and community development having worked for the South Bronx Overall Economic Development Corporation and at Charlotte Center City Partners. Jeremy also worked in the private sector as a consultant for the downtown master plans of Schenectady, NY and his hometown of Asheville, NC. Jeremy received a Master’s in Public Administration from the University of Colorado and a B.A. in Economics from the University of North Carolina at Charlotte.

Leadership & Team

Leah Baldwin

Chief of Strategy & Administration

Contact

lbaldwin@downtownpittsburgh.com

(412) 325-0155

Bio

Chief of Strategy and Administration, Leah is responsible for creating, implementing, and overseeing the financial and administrative policies and systems needed to support the operations of the organization including accounting and budgeting, financial reporting, and human resource administration.

Prior to joining the PDP, Leah worked as the Deputy Executive Director of Habitat for Humanity of Greater Pittsburgh. In this role, she led the financial and operational functions of the affiliate as it executed its mission to provide affordable housing for Pittsburgh families. She has also worked as an auditor for non-profit and government organizations with Yeo & Yeo, PC in Kalamazoo, MI.

Leah returned to Pittsburgh after spending time in Chicago and Michigan. She holds a B.A. in accounting, a CPA license, and an MBA from the Katz School of Business at the University of Pittsburgh.

Andrew Bowie

Event Operations Specialist

Contact

abowie@downtownpittsburgh.com

Bio

As Events Operations Specialist,
Andrew

Bowie
manages the on-site execution of the Pittsburgh Downtown Partnership’s signature programming. From large-scale productions like the NFL Draft to recurring events like farmer’s markets.

A Pittsburgh native and Eagle Scout originally from Shaler,
Andrew
was drawn to the PDP for his love of local events and interacting with the community. Prior to joining the PDP he worked as an intern for Allegheny County in their Special Events and Parks Departments.

He holds a Bachelor of Arts in Applied Communication Studies from Kent State University, where he worked on campus in philanthropic fundraising and student journalism.

Tosh Chambers

Director of Mobility

Contact

tchambers@downtownpittsburgh.com

(412) 325-0154

Bio

As Director of Mobility, Tosh is responsible for the development of mobility and infrastructure in Downtown Pittsburgh, spanning from right-of-way improvement projects to transportation demand management programming.
Prior to joining PDP, Tosh served as the Program Director of Move PGH, where he coordinated a consortium of transportation service providers to produce Pittsburgh’s first Mobility as a Service offering. This program built off of his previous work with the City of Pittsburgh’s Department of Mobility and Infrastructure, where he drafted formational policies related to shared mobility service operation. At DOMI he also developed projects, policies, and programs related to smart curb management, electric vehicle charging, and transit integration. Proceeding his time at DOMI, Tosh worked with Argo AI and Pittsburgh Regional Transit in mapping, policy development, and data analysis.
Tosh hails from Lancaster, PA and migrated to the Iron City to attend the University of Pittsburgh, where he graduated with a BA in Environmental Studies and a concentration in Geography.

Bruce Chan

Senior Director of Urban Design

Contact

bchan@downtownpittsburgh.com

(412) 325-0158

Bio

Joining the Pittsburgh Downtown Partnership in February 2022, Bruce Chan came to the organization during a time when the world recognized that cities need a vibrant, accessible, and healthy public realm, especially in the face of an ongoing pandemic and small business distress. As the Senior Director of Urban Design, Bruce is responsible for advancing urban planning and infrastructure projects that improve the quality of life for all in Downtown Pittsburgh.
Prior to joining the PDP, Bruce worked as a designer with local firm Studio for Spatial Practice where he collaborated with local Western Pennsylvania organizations and municipalities in enhancing and updating communities, with an eye towards preservation, accessibility, and equity. He has also taught at CMU’s School of Architecture.
Bruce serves on the Board of the Bloomfield Development Corporation, advocating for affordable housing, safe streets, and green infrastructure. In 2016, he received the Advocate of the Year award from Bike Pittsburgh, where he currently serves on the Board as an advocate for a more bikeable, walkable, and livable Pittsburgh.
A native of Southern California, Bruce holds a Master of Urban Design from the Carnegie Mellon School of Architecture, and a Bachelor of Architecture from the University of Southern California.

Caroline Colantonio

Events Operations Manager

Contact

ccolantonio@downtownpittsburgh.com

Bio

As Events Operations Manager, Caroline Colantonio takes on a leading role for oversight management of the execution of recurring and one-off special events and programming for the PDP.

Caroline was first introduced to the PDP in the summer of 2023 while working World Square, night markets, and Picklesburgh. She was drawn to the PDP’s mission to cultivate a dynamic and immersive downtown through thoughtful and engaging initiatives. As an integral member of the Events team, Caroline ensures the on-site success of the PDP’s downtown activations and programing for the Pittsburgh community!

Caroline has been living in Pittsburgh for most of her life and is truly fulfilled by getting to showcase the city she loves through her work with the Pittsburgh Downtown Partnership. Caroline holds a Bachelor of Science in Business with a Minor in Event Management from St. Johns University in Queens, NY.

Jack Dougherty

Senior Director of Strategic Partnerships

Contact

jdougherty@downtownpittsburgh.com

Bio

As Senior Director of Strategic Partnerships, Jack is responsible for developing and maintaining strong relationships with Downtown community stakeholders, including businesses, residents, and property owners. Jack oversees and manages the PDP’s membership program and plan, and leads efforts to engage the Downtown community and support the organization’s mission. A member of
Pittsburgh Magazine
and PUMP’s 40 under 40 class of 2022, Jack also plays a key role in placemaking strategy in Market Square and other initiatives that support the PDP’s role in enhancing the Downtown neighborhood for all.
Prior to joining the PDP, he served as an AmeriCorps VISTA member in Mayor Luke Ravenstahl’s office as a Civic Engagement Associate, where he was responsible for implementing and managing various volunteer initiatives including launching the Snow Angels Program.
Jack is originally from Chester Springs outside of Philadelphia but has called Pittsburgh home since earning a B.A. in political science from Duquesne University.

Lynda Fairbrother

Executive Assistant & Office Manager

Contact

LFairbrother@downtownpittsburgh.com

(412) 325-0162

Bio

Lynda keeps the PDP office running smoothly and provides administrative and scheduling support to the organization’s President and CEO, as well as the executive and managerial teams. Lynda also assists the marketing department with the PDP’s membership program.
Lynda earned a degree from Art Institute of Pittsburgh and is pursuing another in Interior Design.

Ben Filio

Manager of Public Realm Projects

Contact

bfilio@downtownpittsburgh.com

Bio

–

Barrie Gregg

Operations Manager, On-Street Services

Contact

bgregg@blockbyblock.com

Bio

As Operations Manager, Mr. Gregg is responsible for the daily guidance and direction of our On-Street Services team of up to 20 Downtown ambassadors. He creates and continually develops deployment plans for the PDP’s Clean Teams while assisting with the logistics of PDP events.
Originating from Coleraine, Northern Ireland, Mr. Gregg attended the local Technical College for Civil Engineering and Belfast Met for Accounting. He brings his experience from working as a manager for companies like Wetherspoons, Gateway Food Markets, and Security Site Management, along with financial experience working as a Finance/Grant Officer for the Muscular Dystrophy Campaign.
Mr. Gregg previous lived and worked in Belfast and London, where, in his spare time, he was part of the Social Outreach Team at The Holy Trinity Brompton, through which he assisted homeless persons with housing, coaching, and pairing them with employment opportunities.

Becca Hansborough-Stoudt

Director of Communications

Contact

rhansborough@downtownpittsburgh.com

Bio

As Director of Communications, Becca oversees the PDP’s media relations strategies and plays a key role in further establishing the organization as thought leaders for the Golden Triangle. She also works closely with the digital marketing team to ensure the PDP’s “voice” is consistent across multiple platforms.

A Pittsburgh transplant of now 11 years, in her free time Becca manages an Instagram-based food and lifestyle blog that highlights all things about the city of bridges. She holds an MBA and a master’s in journalism from Point Park University.

André Henry

Events Programs Manager

Contact

AHenry@downtownpittsburgh.com

Bio

As an Events Programs Manager, André Henry assists with the coordination, execution, oversight, and planning of recurring and one-off special events around Downtown Pittsburgh, as well as major events such as Light Up Night and Picklesburgh. In addition, he is responsible for coordinating basic support for non-PDP events in Market Square.
André is originally from Lancaster, PA, and moved to Pittsburgh in 2019. Prior to joining the PDP, André worked as an Operations Supervisor at the David L. Lawrence Convention Center, and then as a Special Events Coordinator with Macedonia Church of Pittsburgh. André graduated from Millersville University with a degree in Communications and minor in Athletic Coaching.

Richard Hooper

Vice President of Marketing & Communications

Contact

RHooper@downtownpittsburgh.com

Bio

Richard serves as the Vice President of Marketing and Communications and is responsible for driving all marketing activities to enhance the image and public awareness of Downtown Pittsburgh and the PDP. Working in collaboration with other senior leadership team members, Richard ensures marketing strategy is an alignment with the brand position, and provides vision and leadership to advance the mission and goals of the organization locally, regionally, and nationally.
Prior to joining the PDP, Richard spent 12 years as co-founder and creative director of Third Planet Communications, Inc., a nationally recognized marketing/communications firm and 8 years prior as founder and design director of Reinnov8 Design Group both based in the Pittsburgh area. He also spent several years as Experience Design Manager and Design Principal with ZEFER Pittsburgh leading a specialist teams in definition and execution of large-scale web strategies and initiatives. British born, his background also includes international experience, having worked for the British Standards Institution and AB design Associates, Nottingham. His marketing/communications work has been nationally recognized by Graphic Design USA, and American Graphic Design and Advertising, for over 30 years.
Richard received a Bachelor of Arts (Hons) degree in Information Graphics/Marketing from Nottingham Trent University in the UK.

Cate Irvin

Senior Director of Economic Development

Contact

CIrvin@downtownpittsburgh.com

(412) 325-0157

Bio

Cate Irvin is the Senior Director of Economic Development at the Pittsburgh Downtown Partnership, where she leads retail recruitment, market analysis, business development, and storefront activation strategies for Downtown Pittsburgh. Her professional background spans transportation policy, placemaking, economic development, and academic research. Cate recently chaired the International Downtown Association’s Top Issues Council on Retail, helping shape national conversations around storefront vacancy and downtown retail recovery. She is a graduate of IDA’s Emerging Leader Fellowship, holds a Master of Public Health, and is ABD in Urban Sociology at Tulane University, where her research focuses on adaptive governance, temporary urbanism, and downtown revitalization.

Wade Larison

Development & Grants Coordinator

Contact

wlarison@downtownpittsburgh.com

Bio

As Development and Grants Coordinator, Wade supports the Pittsburgh Downtown Partnership’s grant strategy, funder communications, reporting, and project narratives tied to Downtown Pittsburgh’s continued growth and recovery.
Prior to joining the PDP, Wade spent three years with the Hill Community Development Corporation, where he supported grant writing, public engagement, and community development operations. His time there also included service through AmeriCorps Public Allies, a national program focused on nonprofit leadership and community-centered work.
Wade holds a Master’s Degree in Philosophy from Duquesne University and an undergraduate degree in Philosophy from Indiana University of Pennsylvania. His academic work focused on technology, time, and the relationship between everyday experience and structures of power.

Christa Lerch

Director of Finance

Contact

clerch@downtownpittsburgh.com

Bio

Christa serves as Director of Finance for the PDP, where she oversees the organization’s daily accounting and financial operations. She ensures compliance with internal control standards to support effective and efficient financial management, and prepares and maintains grant-related, financial, and budgetary reports for both internal and external stakeholders.
Prior to joining the PDP, Christa worked as Finance Manager at the Pittsburgh Cultural Trust, where she oversaw financial procedures for multiple new performance venues. She brings a strong foundation in nonprofit accounting from her earlier experience as a nonprofit and government auditor at the accounting firm Maher Duessel.

Jo Levin

Digital Marketing Manager

Contact

jlevin@downtownpittsburgh.com

Bio

As Digital Marketing Manager, Jo Levin supports the PDP’s digital marketing strategy, including social media, email marketing, website optimization, and online engagement initiatives that promote Downtown Pittsburgh as a vibrant place to live, play, work, and visit.
Originally from Cleveland, Ohio, Jo relocated to Pittsburgh with her 2-year-old golden retriever gal pal,
Stevie.
Jo was drawn to the city’s authentic rust belt character that resonates with her roots. Jo works to better our world through dynamic storytelling to advance purpose-driven advocacy. Throughout her early career, she has developed and implemented strategic and holistic mass-communication campaigns for humanitarian aid NGOs and local and global non-profit organizations. Jo holds a Bachelor of Arts in Applied Communication from Kent State University and an Associate of Arts from Cuyahoga Community College.

Mike Mitcham

Senior Vice President of Public Realm Activation & Management

Contact

mmitcham@downtownpittsburgh.com

Bio

As Senior Vice President of Public Realm Activation & Management, Mike leads a cross-functional team that produces large-scale signature events like Picklesburgh, Light Up Night, and Oktoberfest, while also helping create vibrant spaces full of art, culture, and community that draw people to Downtown Pittsburgh through neighborhood scale activations, public art, and public space improvements. At the same time, Mike oversees the Clean, Outreach & Hospitality Programs, which provide Downtown with year-round litter and graffiti removal, hospitality ambassadors, beautification projects, and social service outreach to support individuals in need. He ensures that with placemaking, public realm management, and on-street services working together, Downtown Pittsburgh is not only lively and engaging, but also clean, safe, and welcoming for all.
A native of Titusville, Pennsylvania—known as “the valley that changed the world,” Mike has been based in Pittsburgh since 1999. Mike’s 20+ year background in hospitality and operations influences his work in making Downtown Pittsburgh the premier place to live, work, and play.

Lynn Morrissey

Senior Director of Special Events

Contact

LMorrissey@downtownpittsburgh.com

Bio

As the Senior Director of Special Events, Lynn oversees PDP’s robust schedule of programming and activations, including the Market Square schedule of Farmers Markets, Night Markets, fitness classes, and music programming, as well as the annual Picklesburgh festival, and holiday programming including Light Up Night, and the Peoples Gas Holiday Market, among many other Downtown events.

Aaron Sukenik

Vice President of District Development

Contact

ASukenik@downtownpittsburgh.com

Bio

As Vice President of District Development, Aaron is responsible for the mobility and infrastructure, economic development, and placemaking work of PDP. This work includes advancing investments, policies, programs and projects that improve the quality of life and enhance economic activity in Downtown Pittsburgh.
Prior to joining the PDP, Aaron spent 10 years as Executive Director of the Hilltop Alliance in south Pittsburgh, where he led work in the areas of business district management and small business assistance, placemaking and open space development (including the Hilltop Urban Farm), residential property stabilization and home repairs, and vacant property recycling and redevelopment (including affordable housing). He also spent several years before that in other local government and community development leadership positions, including as a Township Manager and Business District Manager.  His community development projects and programs have been locally, regionally, and nationally recognized through media and various awards.
Aaron received a Bachelor of Arts degree in History and Master’s degree in Public Administration from the University of Pittsburgh. Though originally from Washington DC, Aaron has lived in Pittsburgh since the dawn of the 21st Century.

Lesalle Thompson

Outreach Specialist, On-Street Services

Contact

lthompson@blockbyblock.com

Bio

As the Outreach Specialist for our Outreach Program, Lesalle Thompson works to connect individuals with the local social service outreach programs, organizations, and agencies within the boundaries of Downtown’s Business Improvement District.

James Wimberly

General Manager, Clean & Safe Program, On-Street Services

Contact

JWimberly@blockbyblock.com

Bio

James Wimberly serves as the General Manager for our Clean & Safe Program, where he oversees the operations of our acclaimed On-Street Services teams whose efforts help build and maintain clean and safe public spaces, connect individuals experiencing homelessness with needed resources, and create a Downtown landscape that helps cultivate strong economic growth.
Originally from Detroit, MI, James holds a Bachelor of Arts in Business Administration and Management, and a Masters of Divinity from the Pittsburgh Theological Seminary. He is also an Ordained Baptist Reverend, and an avid basketball fan.

Anna Wolf

Events Production Manager

Contact

AWolf@downtownpittsburgh.com

Bio

As the Events Production Manager, Anna Wold focuses on planning, strategizing, and executing exceptional events in Downtown. Whether she is communicating with local vendors for markets or helping to bring to life to a certain pickle-themed festival in Downtown, Anna relishes (pun intended) the fact that each day brings new ideas and excitement.
Anna was first introduced to the PDP as a Marketing & Events intern. She was drawn back to the organization for the same reason years later: the opportunity to collaborate with a dedicated and dynamic team that is determined to create a positive impact in the community.

Membership

Our members are a diverse network of stakeholders who share in our vision for Downtown and the region as a whole.
From the ever-expanding popularity of Picklesburgh, to the bustling outdoor dining scene, to dedicated services that keep our streets safe and clean, our mission is to foster a Downtown that is welcoming to all, and our members are vital part of everything we do.

Become a Member

Membership Directory

Accomplishments and Priorities
The PDP has a long history of providing innovative programs and services to improve and enhance Downtown’s business environment, which includes:
Programming
public spaces
and
producing events
to keep Downtown vibrant and active
Encouraging alternative modes of transportation and improving pedestrian and bike safety Downtown
Reducing quality-of-life issues by
providing outreach
services to the homeless and individuals in need
Advocating for transportation funding solutions via the
KeepPGHMoving
campaign
Partnering with the City of Pittsburgh to ensure Market Square becomes a premier public space for Downtown workers, residents, and visitors
Promoting enhancements to the built environment through the Paris to Pittsburgh streetscape and façade improvement program
Conducting
Downtown-focused research
to promote the successes of Downtown and encourage investments to ensure Downtown remains the commercial and cultural hub for the region.

What Our Members Have to Say

“The assistance provided by the Pittsburgh Downtown Partnership has been instrumental in our redevelopment efforts of the Union Trust Building. This has allowed us to recruit new tenants and several new restaurants to this historic Downtown landmark. Their
research, data collection, and expertise
help us to make a compelling case for investing in Downtown.”
Christopher Lasky, Vice President of Development,
The Davis Companies

“As naming sponsor of Light Up Night, Comcast has found the Pittsburgh Downtown Partnership to be a great asset and partner, an organization that works promptly and professionally to help us reach our goals and make the city an outstanding place to do business. The visibility we have achieved with PDP’s help and experience has exceeded our expectations and we look forward to continuing our relationship.”
Christine Whitaker, Senior Vice President,
Comcast

Our Programs

PDP Events & Activations

Innovative, exciting programming to activate Downtown Pittsburgh
The Pittsburgh Downtown Partnership develops unique programs to enliven and activate Downtown Pittsburgh. Our programming comes in a variety of forms including one-time pop-up events, weekly markets in Market Square, public art installations throughout Downtown, and more. We are committed to producing events designed to encourage visitors, residents, and workers to explore Downtown’s unique offerings.

Vendor, Performer & Sponsor Opportunities
The PDP offers year-round opportunities for businesses and artists to get involved with our events and programming.

World Square

Lending For Historic Preservation

As the lending arm of PHLF, Landmarks Community Capital Corporation (LCCC)—a non-profit subsidiary— advances the cause of preservation by extending loans to projects that facilitate renovation activities in historic neighborhoods throughout the Pittsburgh region.

Among the projects we financed recently was a
$200,000
loan to RTH Investments LLC, an affiliate of Rising Tide Partners, to acquire and complete the renovation of a triplex on Flowers Avenue in the city neighborhood of Hazelwood. This project was funded in part by a grant from 1772 Foundation in the amount of $50,000.

This building, pictured here in a before-and-after, was for a short period of time the home of legendary Pittsburgh author August Wilson. The building was renovated on an affordable rental basis for families in the Hazelwood community that have experienced homelessness.

Certified by the United States Department of the Treasury as a Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI), LCC makes sixty percent of its loans in low-to-moderate-income neighborhoods to either for-profit or non-profit developers.

text:
About

History

PHLF was founded in opposition to the demolition of the failed “urban renewal” policies

The Pittsburgh History & Landmarks Foundation (PHLF) was founded in 1964 by a group of citizens who passionately believed that historic preservation, rather than massive demolition, could be a tool for renewing communities, creating pride among residents, and achieving sustainable economic development.

Recognized as one of the nation’s most innovative and effective nonprofit historic preservation organizations, PHLF works to,
identify and save
historically significant places;
renew
historic neighborhoods, towns, and urban areas;
preserve
historic farms and historic designed landscapes; and
educate
people about the Pittsburgh region’s rich architectural heritage.

At the time of PHLF’s founding, vast amounts of public money were being spent to replace some of Pittsburgh’s most historic neighborhoods and commercial areas with characterless architecture, parking lots and roadways. In the 1950s and 1960s in Pittsburgh as in many other cities, “urban renewal” meant destroying much of the existing built environment. Pittsburgh’s “Renaissance” mayor David L. Lawrence was quoted as saying, “The town has no worship of landmarks. Instead, it takes pleasure in the swing of the headache ball and the crash of falling brick.”

It was in this environment that PHLF was born, and as the organization evolved, urban renewal and planning agencies began to alter to some extent their “tear it down” policies. In 1967, PHLF worked with the City of Pittsburgh’s Department of Planning to prepare an historic preservation ordinance for the city, which was adopted in 1971. The Urban Redevelopment Authority commissioned PHLF to do a preservation study of Manchester, an historic neighborhood on the city’s North Side, as early as 1970, and surveys were subsequently performed for URA, the Allegheny Conference on Community Development, and various city and county agencies.

Early success in Manchester

PHLF started its work in neighborhoods on Liverpool Street in Manchester

For PHLF, it all started in the 1300 block of Liverpool Street, in a predominantly African American community on the city’s North Side. There, PHLF established a revolving Preservation Fund and began to work aggressively to save and restore buildings in historic neighborhoods.

In Manchester, primarily a neighborhood of impressive red brick houses with stone trim and wooden porches set on an orderly street grid, PHLF worked with neighborhood residents to create the first historic preservation district in the nation primarily for African Americans; the first preservation program using urban-renewal funds for the restoration of houses for low-to moderate-income residents and a series of incentive programs designed to combat displacement and encourage longtime residents to stay and become part of a revitalized community.

PHLF nominated and listed Manchester on the National Register of Historic Places in 1975 and in 1979, it was designated a City Historic District.

In Manchester, PHLF also helped organize residents into what is now the Manchester Citizens Corporation and in the Mexican War Streets, PHLF began an experimental program, the first of its kind in the nation, in conjunction with the Pittsburgh Housing Authority to restore dilapidated buildings and houses while maintaining affordable housing for the community thus avoiding dislocation of the neighborhood residents.

The organization became adept at innovative financing, simultaneously exploring creative uses of government programs in ways that accomplished preservation goals and developed the assets of the revolving preservation fund generously supported by Pittsburgh’s philanthropic foundations.

PHLF has always preferred to work with and support established neighborhood community organizations, offering services and administering funding for neighborhood projects through established community-based groups.

To that end, PHLF also worked actively with neighborhood residents to form such organizations where none existed like the Manchester Citizens Council and the Mexican War Streets Association, two important civic groups. The most notable achievement of this kind is undoubtedly the Pittsburgh Community Reinvestment Group (PCRG), originally an umbrella organization of community groups founded in 1988. These organizations continue today.

Saving the former Allegheny Post Office building

Beyond Manchester and the Mexican War Streets, one of PHLF’s early and important historic preservation victories on the North Side was the fight to save the former Allegheny Post Office, a grand Italian Renaissance building of 1897 and one of the few public buildings of the City of Allegheny to survive the demolition of the Central North Side. The building was saved when PHLF agreed to purchase and occupy it following a 1969 PHLF proposal to restore the building and transform it into a museum of Pittsburgh and Allegheny County history as well as a vital development centerpiece on the North Side.

PHLF led the effort to save the former Allegheny Post Office building, which now houses Children’s Museum of Pittsburgh

Renamed the Old Post Office Museum, the building served as the headquarters of PHLF starting in 1971 and housed architectural artifacts salvaged from demolished buildings, and a sculptural garden included sculptures that had been salvaged from the former Manchester Bridge, which was demolished in 1970. The building would be the home of PHLF until 1985 when a new use for it was proposed as the home of the Pittsburgh Children’s Museum. PHLF gave the building and garden to Children’s Museum in 1989.

Station Square and Preservation in Downtown

In the mid 1970s, PHLF began its most ambitious and successful program, the redevelopment of Station Square, a riverfront development along the Monongahela directly opposite Downtown Pittsburgh. PHLF conceived the idea in 1975 when there was talk of tearing down some of the under-utilized Pittsburgh & Lake Erie Railroad buildings, which were constructed between 1897 and 1917. Although few Pittsburgh leaders and politicians believed that PHLF would be successful, the Allegheny Foundation, a Scaife Family charitable trust generously provided PHLF with an initial $5 million equity grant and supported the development for two decades.

From 1976 to 1984, PHLF would serve as the prime developer of the site, eventually acquiring 52 acres of riverfront property, where PHLF was able to put its principles into practice:

Historic buildings were reused for offices, shops, restaurants, and entertainment;

Parking was conveniently placed near buildings;

Open squares and landscapes were humanly scaled;

Artifacts such as a paddlewheel, Bessemer converter, blowing engine, and bridge finial were treated as sculpture;

And, for the first time in Pittsburgh, underdeveloped riverfront land was utilized as an amenity for people.

In 1976, PHLF started the acquisition of a 52-acre rail road yard along the Monongahela, redeveloping it into Station Square, an office, retail, and entertainment complex on Pittsburgh’s South Side

Five historic railroad buildings were adapted for new uses, and a hotel, a dock for the Gateway Clipper fleet, and parking areas were added. PHLF developed Station Square without using city, county, or state funds, and repaid a federal loan ahead of schedule. The total investment by PHLF and its sub-developers was over $100 million. Upon completion of Station Square, PHLF had taken a site that generated $47,000 in real estate and nothing in parking taxes to one that produced $4 million a year in real estate and parking taxes, created 3,000 jobs, with 143 businesses.

When PHLF sold Station Square in 1994 because its historic preservation goals had been achieved, the sale proceeds of about $25 million plus continuing economic participation were added to funds that help continue the organization’s work in neighborhood revitalization, historic preservation programs, and educational activities. PHLF is only one of few such organizations in the preservation field that has been able to generate revenue while putting its mission to practice.

Now owned by Forest City Enterprises, Inc., a Cleveland-based real estate developer, Station Square continues to be a popular Pittsburgh destination, which offers commercial office space, entertainment, parking convenient to Downtown Pittsburgh, riverboat entertainment, and other amenities.

The work continues…

Activist, innovative, practical, fiscally prudent and resourceful, persistent, flexible, and egalitarian: these qualities characterize PHLF’s commitment to preservation of the past. Through its work, PHLF is improving the quality of life for Pittsburghers and attracting tourists to the region.

In Downtown Pittsburgh, PHLF continues displaying those characteristics and principles through preservation easements that protect buildings, restoration that creates commercial retail spaces and housing in historic buildings, and is helping to renew the economic vitality of the central business district.

PHLF’s Market at Fifth development helped revitalize Downtown’s Market Square

In 2015, PHLF, together with private developers, the City of Pittsburgh’s Urban Redevelopment Authority, the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, other nonprofit organizations and small business owners are all contributing to the burst of renovation activity that is creating a stimulating and economically vital downtown with national architectural distinction.

To that end, PHLF completed the restoration of 11 historic facades on 10 buildings in the core business district of Downtown in 2015, helped launch a new grocery store—Market Street Grocery— the first of its kind back in Downtown’s Market Square for many years, and is working on upper floor development of spaces in historic buildings in Market Square and on Wood Street.

Broad Historic Restoration Program in Wilkinsburg

In Wilkinsburg, a low-to moderate-income bedroom community six miles due east of Downtown, PHLF is continuing a comprehensive historic preservation initiative in partnership with Allegheny County, the Wilkinsburg Community Development Corporation with funding from TriState Capital Bank, through a state tax credit initiative, the Neighborhood Partnership Program.

Over the last 10 years, PHLF’s work in the Hamnett Place neighborhood, a National Register-listed historic district saw the restoration of seven single-family houses, which were sold to new residents, two apartment buildings that provided 27 units of affordable housing and the creation of two gardens on formerly blighted vacant lots.

The restored Crescent Apartments building is a major part of PHLF’s broad historic restoration efforts in Wilkinsburg

In addition, PHLF restored a former auto repair shop into a state-of-the-art learning and meeting space now known as the Landmarks Preservation Resource Center, where the organization offers demonstration workshops on DIY house restoration techniques, seminars, lectures, and film screenings on historic preservation, architectural history, urban planning and community development.

In 2015, PHLF will start restoration work on the Falconhurst Neighborhood Restoration Development Program, a multi-site project that will create 33 more affordable housing units and newly constructed buildings in the Hamnett Place neighborhood.

Through it all, the work of PHLF continues to be guided by the principles of place making espoused by its leader and co-founder, Arthur Ziegler when he notes that, “through the place, we renew the spirit of the people. Historic preservation can be the basis of community renewal, human renewal, and economic renewal. Preservation is not some isolated cultural benefit.”

Today, historic buildings in Downtown, homes in neighborhoods such as Manchester, on Pittsburgh’s North Side, stores on main streets such as East Carson, on the South Side, and the historic buildings housing shops and restaurants at Station Square, a 51-acre former railroad yard, and restored houses in Wilkinsburg, survive and flourish and attract people by their architectural uniqueness, human scale and urban character, thanks in large part to the work and determination of this organization.

Although its primary focus is on the Pittsburgh area, the Pittsburgh History & Landmarks Foundation is chartered to work within a 250-mile radius of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.

PHLF includes subsidiaries:

Landmarks Community Capital Corporation (LCCC), a non-profit lending subsidiary, which makes loans and obtains grants and investment capital, used to finance and develop projects that assist in the revitalization of urban centers, towns, and neighborhoods.

Landmarks Development Corporation (LDC), a for-profit real estate development company that provides consulting services and develops real estate.

PHLF is supported by more than 2,000 members, and guided by 25 trustees, with 23 staff members and more than 75 volunteers.

Through The Place

A feature-length documentary that highlights the history, achievements, and impact of the Pittsburgh History & Landmarks Foundation (PHLF), on Pittsburgh and on preservation in America, since the organization’s founding in Manchester on the North Side of Pittsburgh, in 1964.

“Pittsburgh was probably the first city in the country to go headlong, mistakenly, into the urban renewal mode, bulldozing so much of the fabric of its city as well as its economic heart. So it’s somewhat ironic that Pittsburgh also became the leader in the preservation movement through Arthur Ziegler and the Pittsburgh History & Landmarks Foundation.”

ROBERTA BRANDES GRATZ

Author, "The Living City"

Urban Critic

Determined to preserve the character of their homes, residents of Manchester on Pittsburgh’s North Side, together with the Pittsburgh History & Landmarks Foundation, insisted that renewal efforts be based on preservation.

Founded by a group of citizens who passionately believed that historic preservation, rather than massive demolition, could be a tool for renewing communities, creating pride among residents, and achieving sustainable economic development, PHLF is now recognized as one of the nation’s most innovative and effective nonprofit historic preservation organizations.

In THROUGH THE PLACE, you will see the context of how of PHLF started and learn about its work in saving and restoring important buildings in Pittsburgh neighborhoods and its Main Street business corridors. You will see the breadth of PHLF’s education and preservation programs, which enhance the organization’s advocacy for the preservation of historic buildings and structures in Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, and in America.

Pittsburgh’s historic lower Hill District circa 1954 and the massive distruction that followed during the era of “urban renewal."

Watch the Film Here »

“You’ve got the whole history of American architecture spelled out within walking distance, just in Downtown Pittsburgh. And it has to be saved. It has to be preserved.”

DAVID McCULLOUGH

Author, “The Wright Brothers”

American Historian

Order your copy today!

Available on DVD and Blu-ray.

Visit Store

Produced in association with:

Behind the Camera

In the making of THROUGH THE PLACE, we interviewed a cross-section of leaders of leaders in preservation, including architects, historians, urban and social critics, and leaders of major preservation, civic, and cultural organizations. Through it all, our story took us across three states, filming important landmarks and places, some of which are highlighted in the photo gallery.

Meet the Filmmakers

KARAMAGI RUJUMBA

Producer

View Biography

Karamagi Rujumba

Producer

Karamagi Rujumba is the director of communications and advocacy for the Pittsburgh History & Landmarks Foundation. He coordinates all media and public affairs and represents PHLF on preservation issues at all levels of community and government engagement. He also manages and creates programming for the Landmarks Preservation Resource Center, in Wilkinsburg, Pennsylvania, where PHLF is involved in an expansive house restoration and preservation initiative.

A naturalized American, Karamagi was born in Nairobi, Kenya, and grew up in Uganda before moving to the United States. He is a graduate of Wittenberg University in Springfield, Ohio, where he studied English and Political Science, and also holds a Master of Science degree from Columbia University’s Graduate School of Journalism.

He was a general assignment, government, and education reporter for both the Toledo (Ohio) Blade, and Pittsburgh Post-Gazette newspapers before joining PHLF in October 2010.

DANIEL LOVERING

Director, Videographer, and Editor

View Biography

Daniel Lovering

Director, videographer, and editor

Daniel Lovering is a journalist, photographer and documentary filmmaker based in Cambridge, Massachusetts. He is the founder and principal of
Bagamor Media
, which produces short documentaries and films for media organizations, nonprofits, educational institutions and businesses.

An experienced journalist, Daniel has reported from more than a dozen countries. His writing has appeared in The New York Times, The Economist and Foreign Policy, among other publications. He worked as a staff writer for The Associated Press in Asia and the United States, covering subjects ranging from business and politics to war and natural disasters, and has contributed to Reuters.

From 2005 through 2011, Daniel worked in Pittsburgh as a national business writer for the AP and freelance journalist. He wrote a seven-part series on entrepreneurship in the region for PittsburghTODAY, an initiative of the Regional Indicator program at the University of Pittsburgh’s University Center for Social and Urban Research.

A skilled narrative and visual storyteller, Daniel began his career in film and television production. He graduated from Oberlin College and the Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism and is the recipient of numerous journalism fellowships, including a 2014 Metcalf Institute Fellowship for Marine & Environmental Reporting and a 2012 Knight Luce Fellowship for Reporting on Global Religion.

Bring
Through the Place
to your Classroom

This documentary is both an advocacy and educational tool about the impact of historic preservation as a means of achieving social, cultural, and economic equity in the renewal of America’s historic neighborhoods and urban communities. PHLF is pleased to partner with community organizations, schools, and individuals interested in screening the film as an educational program.

ARTHUR P. ZIEGLER, JR.

Our Mission

Landmarks Community Capital Corporation (LCC) initiates and expands community revitalization by providing creative financing and technical assistance in historic low- to moderate-income neighborhoods and urban centers in Western Pennsylvania. It is a non-profit subsidiary of Pittsburgh History & Landmarks Foundation (PHLF).

Certified by the U.S. Department of the Treasury as a Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI), LCC provides loan capital to both non-profit and for-profit developers for the purpose of purchasing and rehabilitating affordable housing and commercial buildings.

Building upon PHLF’s record of historic preservation since 1964, LCC offers unique capabilities to community development financing with in-house expertise in real estate, construction, and commercial lending.

Town Hall Commons: A Hive of Activity

August 21, 2026 3:39 pm

$350,000 Landmarks loan helps fund restoration of former Ambridge Municipal Building

David Pollino stands outside Town Hall Commons on Merchant Street.

By Anna Samuels

Archivist & Librarian

Walking into the Town Hall Commons development, previously the Ambridge Municipal Building, feels like stepping back in time. Many of the frosted glass doors still bear city department titles, advertisements found in the basement, which are now framed, lean against walls, and four Barnes Safe & Lock Company safes command attention throughout the building. Some of those safes are still in good working order.

The fact that the building has maintained its period accuracy has been beneficial to helping imagine its redevelopment, contends David Pollino, a co-owner of the development. He noted that the building was a filming location for various television shows including
Mindhunter
and
American Rust
, said Pollino as he pointed out the fictional “Buell Police” sign on one door.

Pollino, who had also been looking for investment properties in Bellevue and Coraopolis, was initially interested in a different Ambridge building when the borough’s former municipal building became available.

Town Hall Commons as seen from 10th Street.

The building was too large for Pollino to manage on his own, but with the help of a
$350,000 loan
from Landmarks Community Capital (LCC) — a non-profit lending subsidiary of Pittsburgh History & Landmarks Foundation— and also with the help of Aaron Bryant, his longtime friend and business partner in California, he became the proud co-owner of the c. 1917 building.

Pollino and Bryant’s Town Hall Commons development joins a host of new businesses along Ambridge’s Merchant Street, including a brewery, a café, a wood-fired pizza restaurant, and a newly refurbished German bar.

Designed by James T. Steen, the Classical Revival structure is a three-story brick building that features 14-foot ceilings, exposed interior brick, and arched windows. When Pollino’s aunt, a 90-year-old school teacher, visited from California, she pointed out the intentional architectural details throughout the space explaining; “All these things mean something.”

This beehive-shaped finial represents a hard-working community of workers

The beehive-shaped finial atop a newel post suggests a hardworking community, a perfect visual representation of a steel-making town. The beehive is also a fitting symbol for the building which once housed the police department, fire department, city council, and jail.

When completed, the building will continue to hum with activity, housing office space on the first floor and residential space on the second floor. While apartments are the long-term plan, the space may initially be used for Airbnb rentals.

Pollino and Bryant’s wives have plans for a distillery in the adjoining garage space, which initially housed the fire department, and potential tasting rooms in the basement jail cells.

The building’s name, Town Hall Commons, comes from the original use of the spacious attic level which a 1909 newspaper article described as a gathering space for 350 to 400 people. Pollino and Bryant haven’t decided how this floor will be used, but have discussed an event or shared tenant space.

The LCC loan has helped Pollino and Bryant maintain a high level of quality while renovating the building. It was important to both of them to create a space where they’d want to rent an office space or spend the night. The importance of quality craftsmanship honors the original architectural work evident in the structure. Pollino comments that original details have stood the test of time while some pieces from thirty years ago have had to be replaced.

Ambridge residents are excited to see someone caring for the grand building on Merchant Street. Pollino has received support from the community and borough, which paid for a Phase I inspection with EPA grant funding.

Jail cells in the basement of the building.

The owner of the local antique store directed Pollino and his architect to the Laughlin Memorial Library where the library director gave them a tour of the archives and they poured over historical images of the building.

As the stewards of Town Hall Commons, Pollino and Bryant are ready to shepherd the building into the future.

Check out some more vantage points of the building in the gallery below.

Committee Awards Nine Historic Landmark Plaques

July 1, 2025 2:36 pm

The Historic Plaque Designation Committee of our organization awarded nine plaques — seven individual buildings and two districts — to places worthy of recognition for their architecture, history, and planning, at its June 12 meeting.

The districts are a contrast of significant architecture and significant planning. In what we are referring to as the “
Boundary-Beaver Streets
” Historic District, in Sewickley, significant residential architecture is most evident. The district encompasses both sides of Beaver Street to Nevin Avenue on the west, Centennial Avenue on the north, and Boundary Street on the east.

The boundary coincides with the Sewickley Historic District #2, which our organization worked with the Borough of Sewickley and the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission’s State Historic Preservation Office, to identify and designate in 1985, containing 19 parcels.

This group of 19 houses in eclectic styles reflects the residential taste of a wealthy turn-of-the-century suburb. The works of prominent Pittsburgh architects Alden & Harlow, MacClure & Spahr, and Neal & Rowland are notably represented.

Drawings and Archives, Avery Architectural & Fine Arts Library, Columbia University.

In contrast to the lavish residential architecture of Sewickley, we turn to the modest multi-unit residences contained in
Shalercrest
, now a cooperative housing development, located in the southeastern corner on Shaler Township along Mt. Vernon Drive.

Its 251 units in 59 buildings were developed as Defense Worker Housing by the Federal Works Agency in conjunction with the Allegheny County Housing Authority from 1941 to 1944. It also includes an administrative building, community building, and a former grocery (now apartments), along with recreational fields in the hollow at the center of the development.

The design and planning are the work of architect Clarence S. Stein, the renowned proponent of “Garden City” development. Locally, he may be best known for his planning of Chatham Village with Henry Wright. But here in Shaler Township, and his now gone ‘Ohio View Acres,’ his skill at siting a democratic community on a strict budget and time constraint is evident.

In addition to the two districts, the Committee awarded seven new individual building plaques, which are listed below in order of construction date:

“Farmhouse” at Christ Church at Grove Farm, originally
William and Davidson Duff house
. 249 Duff Road, Ohio Township. c.1835. William Duff, builder, additions.

William W. Grier house.
220 8th Street, Oakmont. 1875. William W. Grier, builder.

Porter & Donaldson Millinery and Straw Goods
building. 820 Liberty Avenue, in Downtown. 1881. James J. Porter, builder.

House.
5906 Callowhill Street
, Highland Park. 1893. Frederick C. Sauer, architect.

First Unitarian Church of Pittsburgh
. 604 Morewood Avenue, Shadyside. 1902-04. Joseph L. Neal of Neal & Rowland, architects.

Liberty School
, now Pittsburgh Liberty K-5. 601 Filbert Street, Shadyside. 1911, 1936-37 addition. Edward J. Weber, designer with MacClure & Spahr, architects. M. M. Steen, board architect for addition.

Imani Christian Academy, originally
East Hills Elementary School
. 2150 East Hills Drive, East Hills. 1969-72. Tasso Katselas, architect.

Our organization has awarded 634 Historic Landmark Plaques since 1968
. A Historic Landmark plaque identifies the site as a significant part of our local heritage. It will not protect a building from alteration or demolition. Buildings, structures, districts, and landscapes may be approved for a Historic Landmark plaque if all of the following conditions are met:

they are remarkable pieces of architecture, engineering, construction, landscape design, or planning, or impart a rich sense of history;

alterations, additions, or deterioration have not substantially lessened their value in the above respects;

they are at least 50 years old and are located within Allegheny County or surrounding counties (see above).

they are not located in historic districts bearing a plaque (unless of exceptional individual significance).

frank@phlf.org
or 412-471-5808 ext. 525.

Landmarks Scholarship award recipients together with their parents and members of the Scholarship Committee posed for a photo at the historic Mansions on Fifth Hotel in Shadyside.

Our organization was delighted to host our Landmarks Scholarship Awards reception at the historic Mansions on Fifth Hotel in Shadyside on June 17.

In this, our 27th year of this scholarship program, our organization awarded three scholarships and five Honorable Mention-awards to college-bound students in Allegheny County who care deeply about the history and distinctive built environment of our city and region.

This year’s awards, makes it
94 scholarships
and

that our organization has awarded to high school graduates in Allegheny County since the program’s inception in 1999.  This program has helped to introduce young people to the work and mission of our organization and has created a network of support and a sense of family among the recipients.

The scholarship award of

, while the
Honorable Mention award is a one-time gift of $250
, payable to the recipient’s college or university for tuition and book expenses.

Aviv Davidson of Pittsburgh Allderdice, will attend American University

We were delighted to interact with our scholarship and honorable mention winners, together with past scholarship recipients, Scholarship Committee members, staff and members of our organization’s Board of Trustees.

David Brashear, who chairs the Scholarship Committee, and initiated the Landmarks Scholarship Program with funding through a PHLF Named Fund, presided over the event and congratulated award recipients along with their parents on the submission of essays that reflect their love of our city and region, and its built environment.
